title: MVC and Layers in an API
section: How an Express API Is Built
summary: See why an API splits into routes, controllers, services, repositories, models, and views, and follow one request through each layer.
intro: Small Express apps put everything in the route handler. That works until two routes need the same rule, a test has to run without a database, or a renamed column breaks every client. Layers fix this by giving each kind of code one home. This lesson follows a request through every layer of StagePass, then compares it with Cookbook, an API in the classic MVC folder layout that most MERN codebases use.

steps.title: One request through every layer
steps.body:
In MVC for an API, the **model** is your data and its rules, the **view** is the JSON that clients get, and the **controller** turns HTTP into calls. Real codebases split the model further, so a request passes through these layers, in this order only:

1. The **route** matches the method and path, and runs middleware.
2. The **controller** reads the validated input and calls a service.
3. The **service** applies the business rules.
4. The **repository** runs the queries.
5. The **view** shapes the result into JSON on the way out.

Each layer only calls the one below it. A service never imports Express, and a controller never builds SQL. StagePass keeps a feature's layers together in one folder. `src/modules/venues/` is the smallest complete feature, and the one to copy when you add a new one. Here is `POST /v1/venues`, from the controller down.

examples.title: The controller
examples.prompt: `create` is the whole HTTP side of `POST /v1/venues`.
examples.explanation: The route already ran `validate({ body: CreateVenue })`, so `req.body` holds the parsed value. The controller calls `this.#venues.create(...)` and picks the answer: `201`, a `Location` header, and `toVenueJson(venue)`. That view is one small function in `venues.view.ts` that lists exactly the fields clients see, so a new database column never leaks into the API by accident.

examples.title: The service
examples.prompt: The rules for venues. Look for anything about HTTP: there is none.
examples.explanation: The service gets its repository and database through the constructor instead of importing them. That is dependency injection: `server.ts` passes the PostgreSQL repository, and tests pass an in-memory fake. A missing venue breaks a rule, so the service throws `NotFoundError` and lets the error handler turn it into a 404. It also owns a cache of single venues: `get` fills it, and `update` deletes the entry so `GET` never serves the old name.

examples.title: The repository
examples.prompt: The interface is what the service depends on. The object under it is the PostgreSQL version, written with Drizzle.
examples.explanation: Every venue query lives in this file, so a slow query or a schema change has one place to look. Each method takes `db` as its first argument, typed `DbOrTx`, so the same query can run alone or inside a transaction. The database refuses a second venue with the same name in the same city, and `translateDuplicate` turns that error (PostgreSQL code `23505`) into a `ConflictError`, a 409 that explains itself instead of a raw database error.

steps.title: Services, interfaces, and wiring
steps.body:
A service is where the rules live: who may do what, which states an object may move between, and which writes must happen together. It never sees `req` or `res`, so a route, a script, or a test can call it the same way.

Services depend on repository **interfaces**, not on PostgreSQL. One file, `src/services.ts`, builds every service and hands each one its repositories. `server.ts` gives it the PostgreSQL repositories, and the tests give it in-memory fakes from `test/support/fakes.ts`. The services cannot tell the difference, and that is the point.

Broken rules travel back up as errors. A service throws `ConflictError` or `NotFoundError`, the controller does nothing special, and the error handler picks the status code. Each layer keeps to its one job.

examples.title: The rules for publishing
examples.prompt: Publishing an event has three conditions. Find each one.
examples.explanation: The method locks the event inside a transaction, then checks the rules in order: only a draft can be published, it must start in the future, and it needs at least one ticket type. Each broken rule throws a `ConflictError` with a short type such as `no-ticket-types`, which becomes a 409 whose `type` clients can switch on. The status change and the `event.published` hook run in the same transaction, so they commit together or not at all.

examples.title: The wiring in one place
examples.prompt: `createServices` builds every service from the repositories it is given.
examples.explanation: Each service gets exactly the repositories it needs, through its constructor. `server.ts` calls this function with `pgRepositories`, and `makeTestApp()` in `test/support/fakes.ts` calls it with fakes. So the API tests run the real services, policies, and hooks in milliseconds, without a database. The hooks are registered here as well, so no module has to know which other modules react to its writes.

steps.title: Classic MVC, one folder per layer
steps.body:
Most Express codebases you join, MERN apps included, group files by layer instead of by feature: `models/`, `controllers/`, `routes/`, and often `services/` and `views/`. Cookbook, a recipes API on MongoDB, uses that layout. The layers and their direction are the same as in StagePass: routes, then controllers, then services, then models.

Which layout should you pick? Folders by layer are quick to start and fine for a handful of resources. Folders by feature, like `modules/events/`, scale better, because a change to one feature stays in one folder. Either way, the habit that matters is the direction of the imports.

In this layout the Mongoose model is the M of MVC: the schema, its validation, and its hooks. A JSON view still decides what clients see.

examples.title: The folder map
examples.prompt: This map from Cookbook's README is the first thing to read in an unfamiliar codebase.
examples.code:
src/server.ts            entry point: connect, build the app, listen on PORT, shut down on a signal
src/app.ts               composition root: request id, pino-http, json, session, routes, 404, errors
src/config.ts            the environment, checked by a zod schema
src/clock.ts, logger.ts  the frozen-able clock (HU_FIXED_TIME) and the pino logger
src/db/mongoose.ts       the connection, strictQuery and sanitizeFilter, command monitoring
src/db/command-counter.ts counts a request's database commands into the X-Db-Commands header
src/models/              Mongoose schemas: the Model, with validation, virtuals, indexes, and hooks
src/models/plugins/      soft delete (query + aggregate hooks) and the shared toJSON shape
src/schemas/             zod schemas for what clients send
src/services/            rules that span models or need the current user (recipes, reviews, account)
src/views/               JSON serializers (the "V" of MVC for an API)
src/controllers/         HTTP in, service call, status and view out
src/routes/              URL to handler, with validate() and requireUser
src/middleware/          request id, validate, require-user, not-found, error handler
scripts/                 the seed and the index sync
test/                    model tests and supertest API tests, one database per file
examples.explanation: Each folder is one layer. `routes/` maps URLs to handlers with `validate()` and `requireUser`, `controllers/` handle HTTP, `services/` hold the rules that span models or need the current user, `models/` hold the Mongoose schemas, and `views/` turn documents into JSON. Only `app.ts` wires them together, so you always know where to start reading.

examples.title: The recipe routes
examples.prompt: The same route shape as StagePass, on a router exported from the module.
examples.explanation: Reads are open, and every write puts `requireUser` first, which loads the signed-in user from the session or answers 401. Each route names its zod schema in `validate()`, so the controller only sees valid input. The controllers are imported as modules of plain functions (`import * as recipes`), a common style when a controller holds no state.

examples.title: A controller of plain functions
examples.prompt: These handlers are exported functions instead of class methods. The job is the same.
examples.explanation: `requireUser` put the user on `res.locals.user`, so `create` reads it there and passes its id to the service. The answer is `201` with a `Location` built from the slug, which is how a client fetches the recipe next. `remove` answers `204 No Content`, with no body. The rule that only the author may edit lives in `services/recipes.service.ts`, not here.

recap:
- MVC for an API: the model is data and rules, the view is the JSON shape, and the controller handles HTTP.
- Requests flow one way: route, controller, service, repository, then a view on the way out.
- Services hold the rules and never touch `req` or `res`. They throw error classes, and the error handler picks the status.
- Pass dependencies in through constructors and build them in one composition root, so tests can swap in fakes.
- Group by feature or by layer. The direction of the imports matters more than the folders.
